title: Build report metrics with math, statistics, random, and collections
sources: Python 3.14 Standard Library: math, statistics, random, collections; reviewed 2026-10-03
masterChecklist: Standard modules: math, random, statistics, datetime, pathlib, os, sys, collections, itertools, functools
whyItMatters: A useful report needs counts, rates, a representative value, and sometimes repeatable sample data. Python already provides these building blocks; installing a data-science package for a tiny report adds needless setup.
simpleExplanation: collections.Counter counts repeated labels. statistics.mean gives the arithmetic average; statistics.median gives the middle value and is less affected by an extreme value. math.ceil rounds a positive fraction up to the next whole number, useful for estimating whole batches. random.Random creates a private pseudo-random generator. Give it a fixed seed for a repeatable demonstration, never for a security token. These modules solve different jobs: counting, summarizing, rounding, and simulation.
mentalModel: Imagine a class attendance report: Counter is the tally sheet, mean is the equal-share average, median is the student in the middle of an ordered line, ceil counts how many full buses are needed, and Random is a shuffled practice deck whose order can be repeated during a test.
outcomes: Count labels using Counter without hand-written branching.
Choose mean or median for an explicitly stated reason.
Use ceil for a whole-capacity estimate.
Use a local seeded Random instance for repeatable non-security practice data.

realWorldExample.scenario: A learning platform summarizes quiz scores and estimates how many five-seat mentoring groups it needs.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: A manually maintained count can drift from the actual records; rounding group count down leaves learners without a seat; a global random seed can unexpectedly affect unrelated code.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Calculate metrics from the source records, round capacity up, and isolate any simulated practice draw in its own Random instance.

workedExample.code:
from collections import Counter
import math
import random
import statistics

scores = [4, 5, 5, 6, 20]
labels = ['Python', 'SQL', 'Python', 'Python', 'SQL']
counts = Counter(labels)
print(counts['Python'])
print(statistics.mean(scores))
print(statistics.median(scores))
print(math.ceil(len(scores) / 2))
practice = random.Random(7)
print(practice.choice(['lists']))
explanation: Counter(labels) counts every label, so the Python count is three.
The mean is eight because all five scores sum to forty; the median is five because five is the middle of the sorted scores. The outlier twenty pulls the mean upward.
Five learners in groups of at most two require three groups; math.ceil prevents under-allocation.
The one-item choice keeps the printed demonstration portable across Python implementations; for a real varied sample, pass several options, but do not assert an exact draw across implementations.
Random(7) creates a local repeatable generator. It is not suitable for passwords or tokens.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Replace the outlier 20 with 6 and compare the new mean and median. Explain which changed more.

procedure: Start with a small list of records and identify whether each metric answers a meaningful question.
Use Counter for categorical counts and check the label spelling before reporting.
Use mean and median on numeric data, explaining what an outlier does.
Use math.ceil only when the business question needs an integer capacity rounded upward.
Keep simulations separate with a local Random instance and never use it to make a security credential.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the mean as the typical value even with an extreme score.
commonMistakes.why: An outlier can pull the mean far from most records.
commonMistakes.avoid: Show the median too, and explain the distribution.

commonMistakes.why: Even one leftover learner still needs a group.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use math.ceil on the learner-count-to-capacity ratio.

commonMistakes.why: This generator is designed for simulation, not cryptographic secrecy.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use the secrets module for security-sensitive randomness.

projectConnection.milestone: Add a cohort-metrics card with counts, median score, and required mentoring-group capacity.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: A five-record fixture produces the checked values, and the UI explains why median and upward rounding were chosen.

assessment.question: Why might median describe the typical score better than mean?
assessment.answer: An extreme value can move the mean while leaving the middle ordered value relatively stable.
assessment.explanation: The worked example's 20 pulls mean to 8 but median stays 5.

assessment.question: Why does five learners at capacity two need three groups?
assessment.answer: The remaining fifth learner still needs a group, so round 5 / 2 upward.

assessment.question: Can seeded random.Random generate safe passwords?
assessment.answer: No; it is for reproducible simulations, not security secrets.
assessment.explanation: Use a cryptographically suitable source such as the secrets module for tokens.
